readerTitle: Three values your staff could actually use on a Saturday night
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (두 매장 레스토랑) + 실제 관찰 (Enron의 가치 선언문, Lencioni 2002) · 소프트웨어는 softwareNote로 다룸
insight: 좋은 가치는 멋진 단어가 아니라, 두 좋은 것이 부딪힐 때 무엇을 고를지 알려주는 규칙이다. 그리고 그 규칙은 리더가 무엇을 보상하고 무엇을 넘어가는지로 진짜가 된다.
misconception: 가치는 회의실에서 좋은 단어를 고르고 벽에 붙이면 만들어진다.

sources.text: Lencioni, P. (2002). Make Your Values Mean Something. Harvard Business Review.
Enron 2000 Annual Report (Respect, Integrity, Communication, Excellence)
레스토랑 시나리오와 금액은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Enron의 가치 네 가지(Respect, Integrity, Communication, Excellence)가 2000년 연차보고서에 실렸다는 점과 Lencioni(2002) HBR 글에서 이 사례를 언급한다는 점을 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
레스토랑 이름, 직원 수(약 30명), 직원 재량 보상 한도 $20 등은 모두 가상 설정입니다.

cards.title: Three values your staff could actually use on a Saturday night
body: You run two neighborhood restaurants with about 30 staff. A third is coming, and you won't be on every shift anymore.
Your managers' first draft of company values: *Quality, Integrity, Teamwork, Passion, Excellence.* It could hang on the wall of almost any business. Let's write better ones, in four decisions.

image.label: A restaurant wall poster of generic value words
image.brief: 레스토랑 주방 뒤편 벽. 'Quality, Integrity, Teamwork, Passion, Excellence'가 적힌 액자 포스터에 먼지가 앉아 있고, 그 앞에서 직원들이 바쁘게 지나감. 아무도 포스터를 보지 않음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where do the values come from?
body: You have one afternoon with your managers and a few long-time staff. How do you spend it?

options.text: Brainstorm the words that describe who you want to be, then vote
options.feedback: You get agreement and ambition, but the words float free of real shifts. Staff will read them as hopes, not rules.

options.text: Collect real stories: moments staff did the right thing, and moments things went wrong
options.feedback: Culture is what people already do. Stories show which behavior you want more of, in words staff recognize.

options.text: Adapt the values of a restaurant group you admire
options.feedback: Fast and polished. But their values solved their problems, and your staff will spot borrowed words quickly.

cards.title: Turn a story into a value.
body: Say you chose the stories. One stands out: on a full Saturday, a dishwasher noticed a nut-allergy order plated with the wrong sauce and stopped it at the pass.
How do you write that down?

options.feedback: Nobody disagrees with it, so it guides nobody. On the next rush, it won't tell anyone they may halt service.
Closer, but still a slogan. It doesn't say who can act or what it may cost.

options.text: "Anyone can stop the line if a guest could get hurt, even on a full Saturday"
options.feedback: It names the trade-off: speed loses to safety. Now a dishwasher knows exactly what they are allowed to do.

cards.title: Three values, each with a price.
body: Each one tells staff what to give up when two good things collide. That's what makes it usable.

breakdown.label: Stop the line for safety
breakdown.detail: Anyone can halt service if a guest could get hurt. Speed loses.

breakdown.label: Fix it at the table
breakdown.detail: Any server can comp up to $20 without asking. Some margin loses.

breakdown.label: Say it to the person
breakdown.detail: Problems go to the person directly, not the group chat. Comfort loses.

cards.softwareNote: The same test works for a software team. "Move fast" says little; "We ship before it's polished and fix bugs in public" tells an engineer what to do when a deadline meets a rough edge.

cards.title: How do the values reach the floor?
body: Say you chose the specific wording. Now 30 people, across two sites and every shift, need to live it.

options.text: Print them in the handbook and on the kitchen wall
options.feedback: Everyone can find them. Few will remember them by week three, because nothing in the routine uses them.

options.text: Open each pre-shift huddle with one real story of a value in action, and use them in hiring questions
options.feedback: A small repeated ritual keeps the values alive, and hiring brings in people who already act this way.

options.text: Ask every employee to sign a values pledge
options.feedback: It feels serious, but signatures measure compliance, not belief. Some staff will read it as a threat.

cards.title: Your best chef breaks one.
body: Say you chose the huddles. A month later, your head chef, the reason for your best reviews, mocks a junior cook for stopping the line over a possible allergen. The kitchen goes quiet.

options.text: Let it go. He's too valuable, and the cook was probably overcautious
options.feedback: You keep the chef happy, and everyone learns the real rule: value number one only applies to junior staff.

options.text: Have a quiet word with the chef later
options.feedback: The chef may change, but the kitchen only saw the mockery. Without a visible response, they'll assume nothing happened.

options.text: Thank the cook in front of the team, and set a clear consequence with the chef in private
options.feedback: It may cost you friction with a star. It also proves the values hold when they're expensive, which is the only time they're tested.

cards.title: A value is a rule for hard choices.
body: Good values aren't nice words. They are **decision rules**: they tell people which good thing wins when two collide, without asking the boss.
Then your actions finish the writing. What you praise, what you pay for and what you let slide tell staff which values are real. Decision 4 mattered more than the other three combined.

image.label: A scale tipping between speed and safety
image.brief: 천칭 일러스트. 한쪽 접시에 'Speed', 다른 쪽에 'Safety'. 'Safety' 쪽으로 기울어 있고, 받침대에 'Value #1'이라는 작은 라벨. 따뜻한 레스토랑 색감.

cards.title: A good statement can't save bad behavior.
body: Enron's 2000 annual report listed Respect, Integrity, Communication and Excellence as its values. Months later the company collapsed in an accounting scandal. Words without consistent action can be worse than no words, because staff learn to distrust them.
Also, three is a limit, not a target. If your stories only support two values, write two. And revisit them as you grow: a rule that fits two restaurants may not fit ten.

cards.title: Write values from real moments, give each a price, then defend them.
list: **Decision 1 · What culture is:** start from how people already behave
**Decision 2 · Values in action:** a value names what loses in a trade-off
**Decision 3 · Rituals:** small repeated habits keep values alive
**Decision 4 · Signs of a toxic culture:** what you tolerate from stars becomes the real rule
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take one of your current values and rewrite it as "We choose X even when it costs Y." If you can't name Y, it isn't guiding anyone yet.
